docs.title: SYNK — An engine that fits you better the more you use it
paragraphs: SYNK builds Atlas, a personalization engine. We started in Korean education. Today we are building the SYNK platform, where one SYNK ID carries you across SYNK apps, and we use the same engine for business services and video production.

It began in a classroom in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia. Every student was good at different things, got stuck in different places and had different reasons for learning. Atlas is our attempt to tailor teaching to each person with technology.

SYNK LAB makes Korean textbooks, learning games and a personalized learning app, and is preparing a one-year course aimed at TOPIK Level 4. SYNK SHIFT gives AI-era lectures on careers and work at schools, companies and institutions, and automates repetitive work with AI for companies that took a lecture. SYNK PULSE makes ads and model videos and grows our own music and character stories. SYNK PATH helps with travel plans and with studying, working and settling in Korea.
The SYNK platform is open now as a web preview. Anything still in preparation is labelled as such on each business page.
To build an engine that fits you better the more you use it — so that anyone, in their 20s or their 60s, gets help that matches their goal and situation when they play, study or ask for advice.

LAB covers Korean education, SHIFT AI lectures and work automation, PULSE ads, model videos, music and characters, and PATH personalized travel plus study, work and settling in Korea. All four use the Atlas engines they need.
LAB — Korean textbooks, learning games and a personalized learning app, with a full-time one-year course aimed at TOPIK Level 4 in preparation.

SHIFT — AI lectures at schools, companies and institutions (including AI career lectures for schools), instructors assigned to fit each request, and AI automation of repetitive work for companies that took a lecture. We are taking enquiries now.
PULSE — product ads, brand films, AI model lookbooks and how-to videos, plus the music and stories of Mongle, Kkamong and Marin. AI profiles, introduction decks and studio rental are in preparation.
PATH — travel days planned around your taste and budget. Study and career support, VR interview practice and help with housing are in preparation.
The four businesses are how SYNK divides its work. It does not mean there are four companies or that all four are fully operating.

The Korean games are available when you sign in with SYNK ID, and the SYNK platform is open as a Windows and Mac Preview and a web preview. PULSE is taking ad and model video projects, and the other services are in preparation.

LAB — we have made eight Korean games and three beginner games, and you can play all of them in SYNK WORLD on the SYNK platform by signing in with SYNK ID. SYNK WORLD keeps supported game progress and outfits in your account. All eight textbooks are written; the one-year course, the learning app and VR interview practice are in preparation.
SHIFT — taking enquiries for lectures and work automation. Prices and the terms for assigning instructors are not set yet, and results at client companies have not been checked yet.
PULSE — making ads and model videos, and making music and character stories. AI profiles, introduction decks and studio rental are in preparation and not taking bookings.
PATH — the VR caregiver interview test is available; VR practice for visa interviews and university life, study and career support, and housing support are in preparation.

Start from what you want to do. LAB if you want to learn Korean, SHIFT if you need an AI lecture or work automation, PULSE for ads, model videos, music or characters, and PATH if you are planning travel or study and work in Korea.
If you would rather try SYNK apps first, start with the SYNK platform. The company’s direction and Atlas are on the SYNK home page and the Atlas page.
The SYNK characters you meet on this website are Mongle, Kkamong, and Marin.
Meet Mongle, with a coral-colored body and stitching; Kkamong, with green eyes and brown fur; and Marin, with a navy helmet and yellow eyes.

I wanted to give every student the attention they needed. When I worked at an academy in Mongolia, I knew each student needed different help, but I never had time to tailor it to each one. I started SYNK to do that with technology.

The near-term goal is for students to reach TOPIK Level 4, and the ultimate goal is to help students who learn this way become leaders. The approach I built for one student at a time is now used in four kinds of work, from travel to company services and video production.
Start by deciding what you need now. Learning Korean, an AI lecture or work automation, video or music, or travel and study plans each point to a different page.
Each business page separates what you can do today from what is in preparation, and what you would receive and on what terms. Looking around the SYNK platform web preview first is another way in.
We do not claim proven effects or superiority over other companies based on the examples on our site. Ask through the contact form or hello@synk.im and we will tell you what is possible today.

The site does not yet show a business registration number. We are preparing a new business registration and will publish the actual registration details once it is complete. If you need confirmation, write to hello@synk.im.

SYNK’s founder is Yuho Yang. He studied architecture and psychology, performed on stage and screen, and worked as deputy director of Skyline Edu, an academy in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia.

Setting the company’s direction, and deciding what to hand to AI and what to check himself, is also the founder’s job.

Architecture taught him to see structure, psychology gave him an interest in how people think and act, and the stage taught him to make something with many people in step. He now uses all of it to build SYNK.

Without signing up you can use SYNK WORLD and two member benefits, Pleasure and the free horoscope. My learning profile and the AI subscription board (PC app) are free once you sign in with SYNK ID, and so are the Korean games. Most of them are in Korean.

Korean games — three beginner games you can start without knowing Hangul, and eight games where you do what you hear and read. In SYNK WORLD you hang out with Mongle and pick up Korean, and the mini-games open once you sign in.
Sign in with SYNK ID to see supported game progress and member benefits in My home. Each program stores progress differently, and anything done before signing up does not move to your account.

Atlas is the personalization engine SYNK builds, and eight engines share the work. They understand the goal and situation (Core, Strata, Trail), fit the content, screens, words and sound to the person (Loom, Vellum, Reed), and check whether it helped (Prism, Temper).

The same person needs different practice when the goal changes: preparing for university, working at a Korean company and talking with family call for different language. Atlas changes tasks and explanations by the goal a person sets and their recent results, not by age.

Core decides what is needed now. Strata maps what to learn and in what order (in development). Trail records the process and the change. Loom builds screens that respond to touch. Vellum gives explanations and hints people understand. Reed handles music and sound for the scene. Prism finds patterns across many results. Temper checks whether it helped.

LAB uses the engines for Korean practice and games, SHIFT for AI lectures and work reviews, PULSE for the picture and sound of ads and model videos, and PATH for travel plans and study and interview preparation.
Atlas runs today in the Korean games, and we are extending it to the learning app and business services. Each service shows what is actually in use.
Core decides what is needed now. It looks at what someone is trying to do and where they are stuck, decides the next step and the help needed, and records why something was recommended or left out.
In the Korean games it picks the next question from the shared learning record, and SHIFT is preparing to use the same judgement in its lectures and reviews.
Loom builds screens that respond to touch. It brings felt textures to life with light and motion for screens and characters, making scenes that react naturally to what people do.
It is used for the screens of LAB games and for scene layout and motion in PULSE videos.
Vellum gives explanations people understand. It offers explanations and hints that fit the current task and the person’s answer — why this practice, and what to look at when stuck.
Trail records the process and the change. It notes which tasks were done and where help was needed, and compares earlier and recent answers to see what changed.
Trail is why all eight Korean games share one learning record.
Prism finds recurring difficulties and differences across many people’s results, and shows which content and explanations need work.
Temper checks whether help worked. After a hint or practice, it checks whether the person can now do it alone, and uses that to improve tasks and the kind of help offered.
This is also where the rule lives that a new method is not rolled out if it makes results worse for any group.
Reed handles music and sound for the scene. It chooses sound for works and learning scenes and decides when to use it — for example, turning it down when focus matters.
Lowering the music while a LAB game plays a sentence, and checking levels and narration before a PULSE video is delivered, are Reed’s work.

Strata maps what to learn and in what order, and it is still in development. It links grammar, expressions and vocabulary by difficulty and learning order, and decides which foundation to revisit when something goes wrong.
Strata is still in development.

It is where you use SYNK apps and member benefits in one place with a single SYNK ID. From the platform section on our home page, you can download Preview 0.4.41 for 64-bit Windows or Mac, or open the web preview. Separate Apple Silicon and Intel downloads are available for macOS 13 or later. Check the chip or processor in About This Mac to choose your download.

SYNK WORLD — tap places in Our Town, such as the café, the convenience store or the bus stop, to learn the Korean used there. Eight Korean games share one learning record, and Atlas picks your next practice from it. It opens on the web (synk.im/world) and in the PC app.
Member benefits — My learning profile, the AI subscription board (PC app), Pleasure and a free horoscope, all free for SYNK ID members. The benefits are in Korean.

One SYNK ID — no separate sign-up for each app, and once you sign in your supported records follow the same account. Keep the apps you open often in My library, and turn on the account library to carry them to your other devices.

What we are building — showing only the apps that match your organization and access, and carrying the interests you choose and the moments you found hard in practice into what comes next. You choose, check and correct what is remembered.

These preview builds do not yet have a verified publisher signature or Apple notarization, so you may see a security notice. On Mac, drag the app from the DMG into Applications. The home page includes instructions for the first launch.

The SYNK platform has four member benefits, all free: My learning profile, the AI subscription board, Pleasure and a free horoscope. Pleasure and the horoscope need no account, and all four are in Korean.
My learning profile — shows what you chose apart from what your practice records show, and lets you open the evidence behind each. Sign in with SYNK ID to see it.

AI subscription board — puts this week’s usage, reset times and billing dates for your AI subscriptions on one screen and recommends the account to use first today. It runs in the PC app, reads only the numbers each service officially reports, and keeps its records on that PC.

Pleasure — who to get in touch with today, birthdays and anniversaries on lunar dates too, and the wedding and funeral gifts you have given and received, kept in one place. Start on the web and sign in to keep it on your account.
Free horoscope — your day by star sign and Korean saju, plus compatibility, the month and the year. No ads and nothing locked; the readings are for light fun.

They fall into three groups: engines that understand (Core, Strata, Trail), engines that fit the experience (Loom, Vellum, Reed) and engines that check (Prism, Temper). Each service uses the ones it needs.
Core decides what is needed now and records why something was recommended or left out. Strata maps what to learn and in what order (in development). Trail records the process and what changed.

Loom brings felt textures to life with light and motion for screens that respond to touch. Vellum gives explanations and hints that fit the task and the answer. Reed handles music and sound, and turns it down when focus matters.
Prism finds recurring difficulties across many people’s results. Temper checks whether someone can now do it without help and uses that to improve the help offered.

Atlas chooses the next suggestion from what you told us and what you actually did. It never guesses from age, gender or nationality, and anything AI inferred is marked so you can check and correct it.

Each program stores progress differently. Guest progress stays in that browser; with a SYNK ID, supported records are kept in your account. Anything done before signing up does not move to your account automatically.

In SHIFT lectures and work automation, material and records are used only for the purpose and consent agreed with whoever made the request. You can find how each service keeps, shows and deletes data in the privacy policy.

docs.title: SYNK LAB — Learn Korean, and get ready for Korea
paragraphs: SYNK LAB is an edtech company making Korean textbooks, learning games and a personalized learning app. We are preparing a full-time one-year course aimed at TOPIK Level 4, and our Korean learning games are available when you sign in with SYNK ID.

Games — we have made eight: Racing, Words in Rhythm, Wind Path, Order Rush, The Teacher Is Back, Entry Check, Blank Slice and Talk Rally. Sign in with SYNK ID on the SYNK platform to play them in SYNK WORLD, plus three beginner games you can start without knowing Hangul.

One-year course — a full-time, in-person course that prepares you for TOPIK Level 4 and for classes and daily life at a Korean university. In every 90-minute class, 30 minutes are group speaking, and native Korean conversation, English classes and K-pop activities are planned.
Textbooks — six Synapse Core books for grammar and two Synapse Talk books for conversation; all eight are written and being prepared for publication.
Dates and entry requirements will be in the enrolment notice, and learning results are not guaranteed.
To help people learn Korean and get ready to study in Korea.

SYNK LAB makes Korean textbooks, learning games and a personalized learning app. We are preparing a full-time one-year course aimed at TOPIK Level 4, and our learning games are available when you sign in with SYNK ID.

LAB is preparing Korean education for anyone who wants to learn the language, with no limit by nationality or where you live. Lessons are planned around where you want to use Korean and how much you can do now.

We are preparing to open the one-year course; the eight textbooks are written and the personalized learning app is in development. Who each course is for, its starting level and how to join are announced course by course.

We first explore what learners want to do in Korean and what they find difficult. We are preparing classes in which students use what they have learned in real situations, receive feedback, and practice again in the next task.

Practice includes asking questions in university classes, explaining what you enjoy, and sharing opinions in team activities. We are preparing different ways to participate, including planning and editing as well as speaking and writing.

The classroom scenes on this website are examples explaining our approach. They are not actual student records or verified learning outcomes. Each student’s learning outcomes must be assessed through actual classes and experience.
SYNK LAB’s textbooks comprise six Synapse Core grammar books and two Synapse Talk conversation books—eight in total. The manuscripts are complete, and we are preparing for publication.

The learning goals for each Synapse Core book are:
Book 1 · TOPIK Level 1 — Read Hangul and introduce yourself.
Book 2 · TOPIK Level 2 — Build basic sentence patterns for everyday conversation.
Book 3 · TOPIK Levels 2–3 — Talk naturally about familiar everyday situations.
Book 4 · TOPIK Level 3 — Share your opinion and explain your reasons.
Book 5 · TOPIK Levels 3–4 — Explain your views on social issues.
Book 6 · TOPIK Levels 4–5 — Discuss specialist and abstract topics.

Synapse Talk Book 1 covers beginner conversation and connects with Core Books 1–2. Book 2 covers intermediate conversation and connects with Core Books 3–5. The conversation books cover material through TOPIK Level 4.

The levels indicate each book’s learning goals, not a guarantee of passing. The manuscripts are complete, but final review and publication are still in preparation. Publication dates and access details will be announced separately.

Sign in with SYNK ID on the SYNK platform and open SYNK WORLD to play SYNK LAB’s eight Korean games and the beginner games. Racing, Words in Rhythm, Wind Path, Order Rush and Talk Rally practise listening; The Teacher Is Back, Entry Check and Blank Slice practise reading.

Racing — hear or read a question and steer into the lane with the answer. It covers 2,000 basic words plus sentence, dialogue and notice challenges, and a right answer fires a booster. The word list does not cover the whole TOPIK 1–2 range.

Words in Rhythm — play two lanes along to Korean songs we wrote, then answer O or X to short sentences and questions. The music drops and notes clear while a sentence plays, and rhythm and listening scores are counted separately.

Wind Path — hear short requests like “take the left path” or “jump the low fence” and move for 90 seconds. Order Rush — listen to café customers and make their drinks, including how many, iced or not and what to leave out. Talk Rally — hear what Mongle says as it hits the ball and return it towards the right reply.

The Teacher Is Back — read the teacher’s requests and tidy a classroom with Marin and Kkamong. Entry Check — read the notice, check each guest’s ticket, bags and words, and stamp pass or refuse. Blank Slice — read a sentence with a gap and slice only the word piece that fits.

Beginner games — in Word Magic you change objects with basic words for size and position; in Your First Shop you hand over water, bread and apples in the right amounts; in Fix the Spaceship two players see different screens and repair the ship by talking.

The games are basic practice for TOPIK I listening and reading. TOPIK I tests listening and reading; writing is in TOPIK II and speaking has its own test. Expressions from the games carry into speaking and writing tasks in class; the games do not assess pronunciation or free writing.

A meta-analysis of game-based second-language learning (Dixon et al., 2022) reported d = 0.50, and a meta-analysis of retrieval practice (Yang et al., 2021) reported g = 0.499 across 222 studies and 48,478 learners. We used them as the basis for recall, instant checking, short voice lines and replay. These are averages from outside research; TOPIK scores and long-term effects of SYNK games have not been tested with learners yet.
Your SYNK ID account keeps supported game progress, coins and outfits. The full path linking classes, games and SYNK TOWN is in preparation.
Students use the Korean from their textbooks in games, and we are building an app that picks the next task from their answers and where they needed help. All eight games share one learning record.

At the start we ask why you are learning, how you like to study, when you want hints and how you want feedback. What students told us, their actual records and anything AI inferred are kept separate, and we never judge personality or ability from a single choice or a favourite character.
Hard expressions come back in new situations, and we check whether students can use them without help. Settings change when goals change, and students can correct anything the app got wrong.
The personalized learning app is in development. We are preparing a Korean patent application for the personalization technology (planned for 2028).
We start with why you are learning and how you like to study, then look at your answers, revisions and the teacher’s observations together to find what you do well and where you struggle.
What students told us, their actual records and anything AI inferred are handled separately. We never judge personality or ability from a single choice or a favourite character.
Settings change when goals or study preferences change, and students can correct anything the app got wrong.

Before class, a dance-trained instructor guides K-POP rhythm and basic movements. During class, learners connect movement with Korean expressions. After-class co-creation is an optional program for students who want to join. They choose a role in planning, scripting, performing, or editing, and can take part without performing or being filmed.

Students discuss what to make, listen to one another, explain their reasons in Korean, and check and revise ideas suggested by AI. Creating something together gives them practice in critical thinking, discussion, collaboration, and responsible use of AI—skills they will need in an AI era.

Before class · K-POP warm-up with a professional instructor — An instructor who majored in dance demonstrates K-POP rhythms and basic movements and practices them with students. Activity intensity and duration are adjusted to students’ physical condition. Learners warm up to music they enjoy and catch their breath before joining Korean class.

During class · Connect movements with expressions — Connect words used in the activity, such as 돌다 (turn), 멈추다 (stop), and 함께 (together), with movements that express their meanings. In the fixed 30 minutes of group speaking within a 90-minute class, explain a sequence or make a suggestion such as 이 부분을 다시 해 볼까요? (Shall we try this part again?). Practice saying what you have learned, listening to the response, and explaining again.

After class · Optional co-creation — After-class co-creation is only for students who choose to join. Teams decide on a topic and format, then students choose roles in planning, scripting, performing, or editing. They can contribute through planning, writing, or editing without performing or being filmed. A dance-trained instructor guides students who choose choreography. Students listen to different views, ask why, explain their reasoning, and compare and revise ideas and wording suggested by AI. By explaining what they made together, they practise critical thinking, discussion, collaboration, and communication in Korean.
Movement before learning, gestures that express word meanings, and activities that involve everyone. Explore the sources behind each idea and how LAB plans to use them.

Harvard Medical School · Naperville · Expert commentary · School practice
Harvard Medical School’s John Ratey explains the relationship between exercise, memory, and concentration. Naperville Central High School ran LRPE, placing physical activity before reading and mathematics classes.
In a Harvard Health interview, John Ratey explains that regular exercise may affect brain regions involved in memory and the neurotrophic factor BDNF. Naperville’s LRPE is a school example focused on this connection between physical activity and learning. A 2013 Illinois Public Health Institute case report describes physical education scheduled before reading and mathematics classes for students who needed learning support.
How LAB designs its classes: This informs our plans for K-POP rhythm and movement before class. We choose activities students can enjoy, then adjust duration and intensity by observing fatigue and participation in the lesson afterward.

Schools on the Move · Finland’s national program
Finland promoted Schools on the Move nationally to add movement during lessons and breaks. School staff reported benefits for learning and the school atmosphere.
Schools on the Move is a program with strategic leadership from Finland’s Ministry of Education and Culture and National Agency for Education, and coordination by JAMK University of Applied Sciences. Rather than a single university experiment, it lets schools increase movement and student participation in ways suited to their circumstances. Official program information and its interim report describe reducing prolonged sitting and involving students in planning activities.
How LAB designs its classes: We connect movement before class with Korean lessons, while preparing after-class co-creation as an optional activity. Roles beyond dance include planning, scripting, and editing, so students can practise listening to and resolving different views.

Max Planck Institute · Vocabulary research in cognitive and brain science
In a 2015 study, participants who performed gestures matching the meanings of unfamiliar words they heard remembered the words better. Meaningful pictures also helped memory.
Researchers at the Max Planck Institute for Human Cognitive and Brain Sciences had participants learn unfamiliar words from an artificial language in several ways. Performing gestures or viewing pictures that matched the meanings helped vocabulary memory compared with listening alone. Watching a movement and performing it produced different results; the connection between the word’s meaning and the movement matters.
How LAB designs its classes: We choose gestures and images that fit the meanings of the Korean being learned. Students use the expressions to describe the order of movements or explain them to classmates, then use them again in cultural projects after class.

These sources inform LAB’s class design. They do not indicate partnerships or accreditation from these institutions, or verified results for LAB’s K-POP classes. LAB’s program is in preparation, and learning outcomes will be assessed during actual operation.

Is after-class co-creation required? — No. Only students who want to join take part in the after-class co-creation program. They can choose planning, scripting, comparing meanings, or editing without dancing, performing, or being filmed. Students decide whether to participate and which role they want.

Has research directly compared exercise and language learning? — A 2007 study by Winter and colleagues compared new vocabulary learning among 27 healthy participants after intense running, low-intensity running, and rest. We refer to it as experimental evidence that exercise conditions can affect vocabulary learning. LAB does not use it as proof of K-POP class outcomes or to claim the same improvement rate for every learner.
You can explore LAB even if you have not decided to study abroad. You can start by exploring a subject that interests you, life in Korea, or something you would like to do in Korean.
We are preparing education that helps learners find the information they need and choose their own direction. Check each program’s information for eligibility and participation requirements.
If Hangul is new to you, start with the beginner games. Word Magic, Your First Shop and Fix the Spaceship start with pictures and sound, and there is no timer at first.

Once you are comfortable, move on to the eight Korean games. Racing, Words in Rhythm, Wind Path, Order Rush and Talk Rally practise listening; The Teacher Is Back, Entry Check and Blank Slice practise reading. Sign in with SYNK ID to play the beginner games and the main games.
For the level at which you could join regular classes, tell us why you are learning and your current level and we will let you know.

Yes, adults can learn with LAB. Regular online classes have not started yet: the one-year course is being prepared as an in-person course, and the Korean learning games can be played online by signing in with SYNK ID.
Tell us what you want to learn and when you are available through the contact form or hello@synk.im, and we will let you know where things stand and how you could take part.

No. A teacher teaches the class. The teacher gets to know each student and sets the direction; Atlas helps by recording the student’s answers and where they needed help, and by suggesting the next practice.

The one-year course is being prepared as a regular in-person programme with textbook lessons and group speaking. Of each 90-minute class, 60 minutes are lesson and practice and 30 minutes are group speaking. Conversation with native Korean speakers and the English classes are taught by people too.

The AI does not teach or grade on its own. The Korean games published so far can be played alone, but their records are not a level or pass judgement, and we have not yet confirmed the learning effect with students.

Start by talking with the student about what they want to do in Korean. Then check how the course is taught, the teacher’s role, the length and cost, and the support conditions. The one-year course is still being prepared, so enrolment dates and fees will be announced once they are set.

When the course opens, we will also explain how we tell guardians what the student can now express and where they need help. What is shared, how often, and who can view records will be set in the course guide.
This question box cannot look up a student’s learning records or confirm guardian access. The Korean games are played by signing in with SYNK ID, and supported game progress stays with that account.
We aim for Level 4 with life after admission in mind. Some universities admit students at Level 3, but graduation, scholarships and part-time work often use Level 4 as the benchmark.
TOPIK II PBT · out of 300 — Level 3: 120–149 / Level 4: 150–189
TOPIK II IBT · out of 600 — Level 3: 191–290 / Level 4: 291–360
What we practise at LAB — Level 3: describe familiar situations and give reasons and opinions / Level 4: compare sources and opinions and explain academic and social topics

Graduation — the Korean needed to graduate may differ from the Korean needed to enter. Sangmyung University, for example, lists TOPIK Level 4 or higher as the Korean graduation requirement for general programmes. Requirements vary by school, department and year of entry.

Scholarships — Konyang University’s tuition scholarship for new and transfer students distinguishes 30% at TOPIK Level 3 from 50% at Level 4. Not every university offers the same, so check your target school’s latest admissions guide.

Part-time work — the Korean requirement for part-time work is TOPIK Level 3 for first- and second-year undergraduates and Level 4 for third- and fourth-years. Third- and fourth-years who do not meet it are told 10 hours a week, 25 hours if they do, and 30 hours may apply depending on certified universities and grades. Check with your school and get permission from immigration before working.

Jobs and visas — TOPIK scores show Korean ability in job and residence reviews, but job-seeking (D-10) and employment (E-7 and others) are different statuses, and Level 4 alone does not get you a work visa.
Based on official information as of 18 September 2026. The scores above are for TOPIK II; speaking is a separate test. Requirements differ by school and person, and passing TOPIK is not guaranteed.

We are preparing education for everyone who wants to learn Korean; eligibility and participation requirements will be announced separately for each program. Before visiting, tell us your location and the program you are interested in at hello@synk.im.

To get students saying what they think in the Korean they learned. TOPIK Level 4 is a clear goal, but we do not stop at the score — we teach Korean students will actually use in class, daily life and work in Korea.
Even with AI, students make the call. They decide who they are making something for, listen to other views, and explain in Korean why they revised their work.
We are currently building the course, textbooks and learning app ahead of opening. Students choose and change their own direction, and learning results are not guaranteed.
LAB builds textbooks, games and a learning app together. Students use what they learned in games and conversation, and teachers and the app pick the next practice from that record.
Textbooks and games — grammar from Synapse Core is practised in Synapse Talk conversations and situation games, with tasks that have a clear purpose such as making requests or giving opinions.
Records and feedback — first drafts, revisions and hint use are recorded separately, and teachers review anything AI summarised against the student’s real situation.
Next tasks — topics, the order of explanations and hints change with goals and records, and hard expressions come back in new situations.

Eight textbooks, Korean games and a personalized learning app. The textbooks are written and being prepared for publication, the games are played by signing in with SYNK ID, and the app is in development.
Textbooks — the six Synapse Core grammar books go up to Level 5 and the two Synapse Talk conversation books up to Level 4.
Games and records — students use Korean by running as told, making the drink that was ordered and stamping what the notice allows. All eight games share one learning record.
Learning app — tasks, hints, feedback and records in one place, with changes to goals or study preferences carried into the next lesson.

Together with PATH, we are preparing VR lessons where students rehearse explaining their study plans in a visa interview, asking for help at school and talking about their experience in a job interview. They are not offered yet.

Visa interview practice — mock interviews where students organise their purpose and study plan and answer questions are planned as part of the one-year course. The point is to state your own plan accurately, not to memorise answers.
Life in Korea and work experience — practise asking questions at school, confirming work instructions and reporting problems or asking for help.

How is a visa interview different from immigration inspection? — a visa interview may be requested by a Korean mission during visa review; immigration inspection is a separate step when you arrive in Korea. LAB prepares students to explain their own purpose and plan; it does not apply for visas on anyone’s behalf or guarantee approval.
VR practice records are not work experience or official qualifications.

Students study toward TOPIK Level 4 while practising what they need to attend classes and live in Korea. The course rests on four pillars — Korean, judgement and teamwork, a portfolio, and interviews and daily life — and every 90-minute class includes 30 minutes of group speaking.

Korean — grammar, listening, reading and writing step by step, with expressions used in conversation and situation games. Early on students use Hangul and basic patterns to introduce themselves, order and make plans; then explain reasons and opinions; and finally practise Level 4 tasks comparing sources and organising opinions.
Judgement and teamwork — students choose topics that match their interests and values for team projects, check AI suggestions, listen to other views and explain their own choices.
Portfolio — self-introduction and study plan, writing they drafted and revised, presentations and the roles they took in their team.

Interviews and daily life — mock visa interviews where students explain their study plan in their own words are part of the course, and VR lessons for unfamiliar everyday situations are in preparation.

After the course — if a student finishes the one-year course and does not reach Level 4 on their first TOPIK, we extend their learning app account free for six months to support online study. Attendance or homework is never used to exclude anyone from this. It is not an unlimited extension of classes or a guarantee of passing.
Textbooks — the two Synapse Talk conversation books go up to Level 4 and the six Synapse Core grammar books up to Level 5. Level 4 is the central goal, not the ceiling of the books.

Native conversation, English and cultural activities depend on the course you enrol in. If you need more help settling in or finding work after graduation, you can ask PATH separately; LAB enrolment does not include all PATH services.

We are preparing to open, along with the course, app and VR programme. TOPIK Level 4 is the course goal, not a guarantee, and the portfolio does not replace official language scores or qualifications.
Learning to decide what to create and whom to create it for, rather than simply following AI output. We help learners use their values to guide choices, work with others, and review the results.

Values and philosophy · Find what guides your choices — Ask what kind of life you want and how you want to help others. When starting a project, choose its audience and purpose yourself. Practice respecting others’ choices while considering how your own ideas may affect them.

Creativity · Find ideas in your experience — Find topics in the culture you enjoy and difficulties you have experienced. Explore several approaches and make a small first draft. Compare AI suggestions, add your own experience and expression, and explain what you made different.

Cooperation and consideration · Understand each other’s roles — In crew activities, share roles such as planning, writing, performing, and editing. Ask what classmates find difficult and adjust participation and schedules together. Activities provide experience in doing your part and giving and receiving help.

Openness · Listen to other views and reconsider — When opinions differ, hear the other person’s reasons first. Decide which feedback to use and which choices to keep, with reasons. We encourage learners to try new approaches and revise their thinking when they find a stronger reason.

Judgment · Check AI suggestions and make a choice — Learn the basics of how AI works and its limits, and check its answers against source material. Compare your own draft with AI suggestions and choose what to use or revise. Also learn the responsibilities involved in handling personal information and other people’s creative work.

Expression · Explain your work and your reasons — Explain in Korean whom you created the work for, your role, and the choices you made. Listen and respond to questions after presenting. Organize both the finished work and revisions to show your interests and abilities through specific examples.

Why Korean and foundational learning still matter in the AI age — You need to read and understand sources to review AI answers, and express your own thinking to work with others. LAB connects discussion, writing, and cultural projects with Korean study for TOPIK Level 4. We design classes that distinguish trying independently, receiving necessary help, and explaining again without help, to see what students have actually learned.

Which sources inform this approach? · Checked September 18, 2026 — WEF’s 2025 employer survey highlights analytical and creative thinking, flexibility, self-awareness, and lifelong learning. UNESCO’s 2024 AI competency framework for students and the OECD–European Union’s 2026 AI literacy framework address human-centered judgment, creativity, collaboration, and responsible use. The OECD’s 2026 education outlook emphasizes that performing well on a task with AI is not the same as learning. LAB draws on these sources and its own educational philosophy to design the classes below. These sources do not demonstrate LAB’s educational outcomes or imply institutional accreditation.
Talk directly with native Korean teachers and use expressions learned in your textbooks. Refine your pronunciation and polite language, and practice answering unexpected questions in your own words.
English classes cover introductions and everyday conversation, then reading, emails, and presentations. We assess Korean and English separately to prepare classes suited to each learner’s level.

Native Korean conversation — Practice making requests, asking questions, and sharing opinions with a native Korean teacher. The teacher identifies points to improve in pronunciation, intonation, and polite language, and helps you express your meaning clearly. You use textbook grammar in conversation and learn which expressions fit the situation.

For example, you ask a professor for a meeting, learn that the time is unavailable, and suggest another time. When the teacher changes a question or condition, you adjust your response. After the conversation, review what was clear and what needs work, then try again. Practice the Korean needed to ask questions at university and request help in everyday life.

English classes — Start by introducing yourself and answering questions in English. Learners who need the basics listen to and say short sentences, then move on to reading in their field of interest, writing emails, presentations, and team activities. Lessons cover checking information and explaining opinions at school or work.

For example, write a message introducing a team project to an exchange student and answer questions about roles and schedules. With the teacher, add missing information and revise awkward expressions, then respond to a changed schedule or condition. The length of materials, difficulty of questions, and amount of explanation are adjusted to the learner’s English level and goals.

What if my Korean and English levels are different? — We assess Korean and English separately. If you are comfortable speaking Korean but new to English, for example, English classes begin with basic expressions. In each class, we review what learners say and write and prepare further practice for difficult pronunciation or expressions. Learners then try the same expressions in a different situation to check their understanding.

Which programs include these classes? — We are preparing a program focused on regular Korean classes and another that also includes native Korean conversation and English. Students who want conversation and English classes can choose a program that includes them. Check enrollment information or ask us about opening dates, teachers, class frequency, and what is included.

Native Korean conversation and English classes are in preparation. The situations above are sample class activities. Opening dates and what each program includes will be available in enrollment information.

LAB prepares learners for both language qualifications and real communication. We broaden practice situations so students can organize what they learn into test answers, talk with professors, and explain their experience in interviews. Our English teaching helps students read materials and work with others in ways that fit their intended major and career.

TOPIK · Put what you understand into speech and writing — Use vocabulary and grammar from Korean classes to answer a native teacher’s questions and explain your opinions. Write up the conversation afterward to compare spoken expressions with the written style used in test answers. Listening, reading, and writing are also practiced separately in the test formats.

Studying abroad · Ask questions, get help, and take part — Practice asking professors questions, agreeing on roles in team assignments, and checking information at university offices in Korean. English tasks include explaining opinions to international peers and reading short materials in your field or instructions for English-taught classes. Practice asking again and checking anything you did not understand.

Career preparation · Explain experience and clarify work — Describe your project role and the problems you solved in Korean, then answer follow-up interview questions. Students preparing for careers that require English also practice introductions, work emails, summaries, and short presentations. Beyond rehearsing answers, tasks include asking about unclear instructions and confirming schedules and results.

What will students take away? — Students build a portfolio of Korean request emails and opinion pieces they have written and revised, Korean and English introductions and project descriptions, expressions refined through teacher feedback, team roles, and presentation materials. Recording original wording alongside the reasons for revisions helps students explain their progress. Teachers use this work to suggest further practice, and students can revisit useful materials before a new semester or interview. The length and difficulty of the work depend on the student’s starting level and chosen program.

How are both languages used in one project? — For example, in a project creating a university guide for new international students, learners ask the university questions in Korean and organize the information they confirm. With an English teacher, they identify useful information in English guides and write a message for students from other countries. With a native Korean teacher, they explain the guide aloud and answer unexpected questions. Students compare AI translations or drafts with verified sources and explain why they chose the final wording.

Do English and native-speaker conversation help with TOPIK? — TOPIK II assesses Korean listening, reading, and writing; speaking is a separate test. We design listening, reading, and writing tasks that revisit vocabulary and expressions used in conversation to support test study. English is not assessed in TOPIK. LAB’s English classes help learners understand English materials and communicate in another language; we do not claim that the English classes themselves raise TOPIK scores.

How do you check language requirements for study and work? — Korean-taught and English-taught university programs may require different evidence of language proficiency. We first check the latest requirements of the chosen university and department, then distinguish preparation for official tests from practice needed to participate in classes. Career tasks are also based on the languages required by the intended role and job listing. Work completed in LAB classes does not replace official language scores or guarantee admission or employment.

When you start and every eight weeks, you choose a goal to work on, then plan and make something with your crew. Teachers look at the work and the conversations and give feedback, and students keep a portfolio that shows how their work changed.

Set your goal — Talk about why you are learning Korean and what kind of life you want. When you start and every eight weeks, choose a challenge and look back on it. Your first answer is not fixed as the right one: if your goal changes as you go, note why.

Plan and finish a project with your crew — Use cultural activities to decide what your team wants to share and with whom. Divide the roles, create a draft, and review each other’s work along the way. Projects are designed so students make real decisions within their roles and see their work through to completion.

Use feedback and try again — Teachers review students’ questions, conversations about roles, and revisions. Together with students’ self-assessments, these help identify what support is needed next. Practice might begin with short explanations when presenting is difficult, or comparing sources when evidence is lacking.

Show your choices and growth in a portfolio — Alongside the finished work, organize your original goal, your own draft, your role, and the reasons for revisions. Prepare materials that let you explain, in your own words, what matters to you and what you have tried, and use them to choose your goal for the next eight weeks.

Sample cultural project · Introducing K-culture to a newcomer — Choose music, food, or a game as a team and ask what someone encountering it for the first time might want to know. Decide whether to use a performance, introduction video, or short guide, and write the Korean script yourselves. A team that values everyone’s participation, for example, can make roles for classmates who find dancing difficult. Coordinate schedules and roles, check AI wording suggestions, sources, and usage terms, then revise in response to each other’s reactions. In the presentation, explain why you chose the topic and format and what you changed. This sample activity connects the enjoyment of culture with choices that reflect consideration and values.

How do personalized learning and teachers work together? — We are developing a way to adjust support and the next task by considering the student’s stated goals, completed tasks, and teacher observations together. We do not judge personality from a single activity or score personal values. Automatically connecting classroom observations with all tasks, carrying learning records across devices, and collecting portfolio materials automatically remain development work.

What experience do you want students to leave with? — The experience of expressing an opinion, listening to others, and completing something together. In the next project, learners choose their roles and the support they need more precisely. For LAB, leadership means setting your own direction while collaborating responsibly with others. We support students in finding reasons for their choices, without choosing their interests or careers for them.

The course connecting goal setting, crew projects, and portfolios is in preparation. The project above is an example of class design, not a record of actual student performance or measured skill improvement.

Of the 90 minutes, 60 are lessons and practice and 30 are group speaking. In the speaking time, students decide what they think first, hear their classmates’ reasons, and then explain their final choice themselves.
Decide first — everyone prepares their own view on the same situation or task, what they would choose and why, before speaking in the group.
Listen and adjust — students take turns, ask again when they do not understand, hear reasons when views differ and agree how everyone can take part.
Explain your decision — students decide what to keep and what to change from their first view and explain why. The teacher helps with expressions and guides students to find their own reasons.

What is the 30 minutes? — it is group time inside the 90-minute class, not an extra 30 minutes, and it does not mean one student speaks alone for 30 minutes. Students speak, listen, ask and adjust together, and the teacher makes sure a few students do not dominate. Difficulty and support follow each student’s level, but the 30 minutes of group speaking are never cut.
These are operating standards for a course in preparation. Cooperation, care and judgement are what the class aims to build, not measured gains.

docs.title: SYNK SHIFT — AI lectures, plus work automation
paragraphs: SYNK SHIFT teaches the skills the AI era calls for at schools, companies and institutions. For schools we give AI career lectures on how to steer a career in the AI era and what to prepare, and as an instructor agency we find AI and AI-career instructors and assign them to fit each request.

When a company that took a lecture wants it, we pick one repetitive task and automate it with AI to help cut fixed costs. In a half-day review we map the workflow together and demonstrate one automation, then agree scope and cost up front, build it and check it every month. Consulting, branding, market research and product testing come with lectures and automation where they need them.

Prices for lectures and automation and the terms for assigning instructors are not set yet and are agreed per request. We do not promise learning results or savings in advance; we check them with you afterwards.
To teach careers and work for the AI era, and to automate repetitive tasks.

SYNK SHIFT teaches the skills the AI era calls for at schools, companies and institutions, then automates repetitive work with AI for companies that took a lecture, to cut fixed costs. In schools we also give AI career lectures on how to steer a career in the AI era and what to prepare for it. We also run an instructor agency that finds instructors and assigns them to fit each request.

Schools, companies and institutions getting ready for the AI era. Lectures and the instructor agency are for schools that want career education to reflect how AI is changing work, companies and public bodies that want staff to use AI in real work, and anyone with a topic who struggles to find a fitting instructor.

Work automation suits small companies paying fixed costs for entry, sorting and reporting that people repeat. Rather than company size, we first look at whether there is one clear task to automate, whether before and after can be compared, and who will check the results.
There are no open courses for individuals yet. If you run a business on your own, you can still ask about automating repetitive work.

Each person leaves a lecture with one thing made. Students take a page on what AI is changing in their field and what they will prepare; staff take a piece of work from their own job and a request–check–fix routine to reuse.

Learning goals, prior knowledge needed, the tools allowed and any extra cost, material that must stay out of practice, and which questions we take are agreed with whoever books the lecture beforehand. We do not present one lecture’s results as every attendee’s skill gain.

In lectures, rather than introducing lots of AI tools, we have people make something with a tool that fits their work and practise checking and fixing the result. Which tools to use, and whether they cost extra, is agreed before the lecture.

In work automation, we split the steps AI handles from those a person checks, and make sure that when AI gets something wrong or stops, it alerts you and a person takes over. We never present features under test as client results.

Because the result alone does not tell you what method was used or whether you could use it yourself. SYNK writes down the methods tried, the failures and the reasons for each fix, so that you can judge the method and take it into your own work.

For example, when we made the site logo we put stitch decoration on both the SYNK letters and the business names, and the letters became hard to read. We kept the soft texture and took the stitches off the SYNK letters only, so the word that has to be read first comes first. The felt characters and objects on screen were designed as things you could hold in your hand, and the Loom engine was built to carry that texture onto the screen.

Today you can see this process on the founder page and on the founder’s yuhobuilds channel. SHIFT lectures work the same way: people try things with real material, check the results and learn to fix them.

SHIFT’s work is AI lectures at schools, companies and institutions (including AI career lectures for schools), an instructor agency, and automating work for companies that took a lecture. Consulting, branding, market research and product testing are taken on to support that work.
Consulting — work out which tasks to hand to AI first, and where a person should check.
Branding — fit lecture material, notices and the screens automation adds to your company’s voice and look.
Market research and product testing — interview the people who will use it, watch them try it, and report where they get stuck.
Yes. SHIFT lectures are planned so that people new to AI can make one thing from their own work. The prior knowledge needed and the tools to use are checked before the lecture.

Work automation can start without knowing much about AI too. A lecture first looks at what can be handed to AI, then in a half-day review we map the current workflow with you and agree what can be handed over and where a person checks.

“What we do” on the SHIFT page sets out, for each lecture and for automation, who it fits, an example, what you get and what is agreed first. There are no lecture materials or textbooks to download yet.

AI news and how to use the tools are on SHIFT’s synkbrief channels (YouTube and Instagram). If you need a lecture or automation for your school or company, tell us the audience and the problem to solve, and we will confirm scope and schedule.

We agree the learning goals, audience and time with whoever books the lecture, then pick practice tasks from the audience’s real work or interests. Lectures are SHIFT’s main work, alongside assigning instructors and automating work.
The tools allowed and any extra cost, and material that must stay out of practice, are agreed in advance, and each person leaves with one thing made and a way to do it again.
Audience, schedule and cost are agreed per request, and this does not mean an accredited course or institutional agreement is in operation.

We do not guarantee the same results. SHIFT’s lectures and automation are the way we have prepared to work, and their effect and the savings at real client companies have not been verified yet. Nor do we claim that using AI makes a business succeed.

Savings from automation are measured before and after under the same conditions, and we tell you what we compared against. We do not stretch one demonstration into a savings figure, and results depend on the company’s work and the people using it.
We agree the scope of each request first, then quote.
For work we can show publicly, we present the fixes as well as the finished result: where we got stuck and why we changed the method, based on the actual work.

There is no collection of the exact prompts we sent to AI tools. The cases do explain what we asked for and what came back. Students’ and clients’ material and private operational documents are not published.

SHIFT gives AI lectures at schools, companies and institutions, runs an instructor agency, and automates work. Lectures come first; when a company that took a lecture wants it, we move on to automation.
AI career lectures for schools — not a general careers talk, but how to steer a career in the AI era and which skills to build. Each student leaves with a one-page plan for their own career.
AI lectures for organisations — staff practise on their own work and leave with one piece of work and a request–check–fix routine they can reuse.
Instructor agency — we find AI and AI-career instructors who fit the goal and audience of each request and assign them. You know exactly which instructor is coming before you sign.
AI work automation — we pick one repetitive task and automate it to help cut fixed costs, in the order half-day review, build one task, monthly care.
Consulting, branding, market research and product testing come with lectures and automation where they need them.

Lectures that leave each person with something made, and automation we stay responsible for even when it stops. A lecture is judged by what people made from their own career plans or work, not by how many tools were shown.

For automation we settle what happens when it stops before what it looks like running: where a person checks, how errors and exceptions are flagged, and who fixes it after handover. Savings are reported only from before-and-after measurements under the same conditions.
In four steps: a lecture, a half-day review, building one task, and monthly care.
Lecture — first, look together at what your company can hand to AI and what should stay with people.

Half-day review — we map the workflow with you, demonstrate one automation on the spot, then send a proposal with scope and cost. You decide whether to build after reading it, and you can stop after the review.

Build one task — scope and price are agreed up front, then we automate one task, including where a person checks and how it alerts you when it stops. Connections to your existing systems are agreed within this scope.
Monthly care — each month we check it still runs and adjust it when the work or the services it uses change. Time and cost saved are measured before and after under the same conditions.

We do not take on system builds that change many tasks at once; we go one task at a time. Where a person’s judgement differs a lot each time, the review looks at whether sorting out the work should come before automating it.
Not as a separate service any more. SHIFT now focuses on AI lectures at schools, companies and institutions, an instructor agency, and automating repetitive work for companies that took a lecture.

If you want AI to take repetitive work off your team, ask us about work automation. A lecture first looks at what your company can hand to AI, then in a half-day review we pick one task we can take on and agree scope and cost up front.
Atlas is not something SHIFT sells separately; it is the technology inside, used to fit lectures and reviews to the people and companies taking them.
Market research and product testing are being prepared as support for lectures and automation; they are not a main service we sell on their own.
User and market research — define who will use it and what they must finish, then confirm their current difficulties through interviews and data.
Usability testing — watch where participants stop and what explanation they need while they try it.
Participants, conditions, consent, compensation, schedule and cost are set within the request. We do not generalise a few reactions to the whole market.

Atlas is not something SHIFT sells separately; it is the technology inside, used to fit lectures and reviews to the people and companies taking them. We are preparing it to choose practice tasks and explanations to fit each student’s interests or each company’s work, even on the same topic.
SHIFT does not build and sell chatbot-style services; it teaches people how to use AI and automates repetitive work. We do not sell an API or engine licence for plugging Atlas into your systems.

No. SHIFT’s work today is AI lectures at schools, companies and institutions, an instructor agency and work automation. An API and engine licensing might be considered far in the future, but they are not part of the current business plan.

The business grows from lectures into automating work for companies that took a lecture. Atlas is not something SHIFT sells separately; it is the technology inside, used to fit lectures and reviews to the people and companies taking them.
We have not set a price list for lectures or automation. We agree the audience and scope for each request, then quote.
Lectures — set by audience and size, length and number of sessions, the practice material to prepare and the venue. When we assign another instructor, their terms are confirmed too.

Automation build — scope and price for one task are agreed in the half-day review. It depends on how many exceptions there are and which services it must connect to, and the price is based on the cost the automation removes.

Monthly care — we agree how often we check and what we fix, and take it on month by month. Fees for external services the automation uses may be extra, and if the work changes enough to need a rebuild, scope and cost are agreed again.
The earlier split into setup fees and operating fees is no longer used.

Not a general careers talk: a lecture for schools on how to steer a career in the AI era and which skills to build for it. Students look at how AI is changing work in a field they care about, then pick the skills that work needs and what they can start on now.

Each student leaves with a one-page plan for their own career: what AI is changing in their field and what they will prepare. Year group and class size, lesson time, and the devices and tools students can use are agreed with the school beforehand.
Schedule and cost are agreed with each school. The lecture does not decide a student’s career for them.

Yes. We hear the goal and the audience of the request, then find an AI or AI-career instructor who fits and assign them. First we show an evidence card for each instructor: whose work they teach, what they have made themselves, samples they can share, and what stays after the class.

You know exactly which instructor is coming before you sign. Running the day, a substitute if the instructor cannot come, cancellation and questions after the lecture are written into the contract only as far as we can really promise.

We do not lead with a headcount or a roster; for each request we find an instructor who fits and show you their evidence card. We have not posted for instructors yet. If you would like to teach with us, tell us your field and what you have made yourself at hello@synk.im. Selection criteria, payment and rights to teaching material will be shared once they are set.

There is a casting book of twelve AI models, and with consent we can create a model based on a company’s founder or staff. AI profiles, introduction decks and studio rental are in preparation and not taking bookings.

SYNK PULSE makes product ads, brand films, AI model lookbooks and how-to videos, from planning to the final cut. We also create the music and stories of Mongle, Kkamong and Marin, and look for partners to license them or make something together.
PULSE makes easy-listening music and video, and stories about Mongle, Kkamong and Marin. If you would like to use or make a piece with us, ask PULSE.
We check that sound and picture fit and flow naturally from start to finish before publishing.

We value enjoyment and the feeling a work evokes, but we do not guarantee that listening or viewing alone improves Korean skills or concentration, or provides therapeutic benefits.
We are preparing our service so that personal listening activity is not collected to build educational, emotional, or concentration profiles.

You can ask about music, video, character, and story production collaborations, licensing, advertising, and ad and model video production. Tell us what work you need, where you will use it, your audience, preferred schedule, and required file formats.

For ad and model videos, it helps to send the six things a project starts with: the brand and the purpose of the video, the audience and the one message, mood, model and scenes to include, the channels and whether it runs as a paid ad, the photos, footage, logos and reference shots you have, and the length and schedule.
Production availability and usage terms are confirmed individually. The contract sets out production, ownership and usage rights, delivery files, revisions, and support.
Public examples do not confirm acceptance of a project or a delivery schedule. Advertising work owned by a client is not treated as SYNK-owned creative work.

A public listening or viewing link does not grant permission to redistribute a work, put it in a video, play it in a shop, or use it in advertising or commercially. Please confirm availability and rights first.
To start an inquiry, email hello@synk.im with the work title, media, location, duration, and intended use. This question panel does not grant permission or make a final copyright determination.

To use or make music with us, ask PULSE.

PULSE music and character stories aim to be something people want to hear and see again. We do not build educational or emotional profiles from what people watch, and we do not promise learning or therapeutic effects.
We make easy-listening music and video, and stories about Mongle, Kkamong and Marin.
Music and video — music and video to leave on while you read, work or rest.
Characters and stories — short videos and ongoing stories built on the three characters’ personalities and friendship, which stay the same in every new piece.

Characters and world — appearance, personality, relationships and stories are managed together so the characters stay recognisable in every new work.
Listening to published works is different from using them commercially. If you want to use them somewhere, please ask first.

Commissioned product ads, brand films and AI model videos are handled under PULSE video production. AI lectures and work automation are SHIFT’s job.

Product ads — short ads showing the product’s details and real use, plus cuts for each channel from the same footage.
Brand films and commercials — one film that shows what the company does and what it does well, with cuts for the website, sales and events.
AI models and lookbooks — product images, lookbooks and fashion videos with the AI model you choose, with colour and fit checked against reference photos.

docs.title: How SYNK works — six principles
paragraphs: We work by six principles: we do not guess from age, we check whether it helped, we keep your answers separate from AI guesses, we make the screens and sound ourselves, we build for long-term use, and if something is not ready we say so.
We do not guess from age — we go by the settings a person chooses and what they actually did, not age, gender or nationality. When the goal changes, the next suggestion changes too.

We check whether it helped — finishing something is not proof of progress. We look separately at whether people can now do it without help and whether the suggestion was right. A new method is not rolled out if results get worse for anyone, in their 20s or their 60s.
Your answers and AI guesses stay separate — what you wrote, what you did and what a teacher observed are kept as the original. Anything AI inferred is marked so you can check and correct it.
We make the screens and sound ourselves — one team makes the felt screens and characters, the music and the voices, so we can fit not only the content but how it looks and sounds.

Built to be used for a long time — people choose large text, shorter explanations or a sound-free mode. Free features compute on the device without an AI server, so they keep running as more people use them.
If it is not ready, we say so — we mark what you can use today separately from what we are still building, and we do not promise effects we have not measured.

records.answer:
Sign in with SYNK ID on the SYNK platform and open SYNK WORLD to play SYNK LAB’s eight Korean games and the beginner games. Racing, Words in Rhythm, Wind Path, Order Rush and Talk Rally practise listening; The Teacher Is Back, Entry Check and Blank Slice practise reading.

Racing — hear or read a question and steer into the lane with the answer. It covers 2,000 basic words plus sentence, dialogue and notice challenges, and a right answer fires a booster. The word list does not cover the whole TOPIK 1–2 range.

Words in Rhythm — play two lanes along to Korean songs we wrote, then answer O or X to short sentences and questions. The music drops and notes clear while a sentence plays, and rhythm and listening scores are counted separately.

Wind Path — hear short requests like “take the left path” or “jump the low fence” and move for 90 seconds. Order Rush — listen to café customers and make their drinks, including how many, iced or not and what to leave out. Talk Rally — hear what Mongle says as it hits the ball and return it towards the right reply.

The Teacher Is Back — read the teacher’s requests and tidy a classroom with Marin and Kkamong. Entry Check — read the notice, check each guest’s ticket, bags and words, and stamp pass or refuse. Blank Slice — read a sentence with a gap and slice only the word piece that fits.

Beginner games — in Word Magic you change objects with basic words for size and position; in Your First Shop you hand over water, bread and apples in the right amounts; in Fix the Spaceship two players see different screens and repair the ship by talking.

The games are basic practice for TOPIK I listening and reading. TOPIK I tests listening and reading; writing is in TOPIK II and speaking has its own test. Expressions from the games carry into speaking and writing tasks in class; the games do not assess pronunciation or free writing.

A meta-analysis of game-based second-language learning (Dixon et al., 2022) reported d = 0.50, and a meta-analysis of retrieval practice (Yang et al., 2021) reported g = 0.499 across 222 studies and 48,478 learners. We used them as the basis for recall, instant checking, short voice lines and replay. These are averages from outside research; TOPIK scores and long-term effects of SYNK games have not been tested with learners yet.

Before class · K-POP warm-up with a professional instructor — An instructor who majored in dance demonstrates K-POP rhythms and basic movements and practices them with students. Activity intensity and duration are adjusted to students’ physical condition. Learners warm up to music they enjoy and catch their breath before joining Korean class.

During class · Connect movements with expressions — Connect words used in the activity, such as 돌다 (turn), 멈추다 (stop), and 함께 (together), with movements that express their meanings. In the fixed 30 minutes of group speaking within a 90-minute class, explain a sequence or make a suggestion such as 이 부분을 다시 해 볼까요? (Shall we try this part again?). Practice saying what you have learned, listening to the response, and explaining again.

After class · Optional co-creation — After-class co-creation is only for students who choose to join. Teams decide on a topic and format, then students choose roles in planning, scripting, performing, or editing. They can contribute through planning, writing, or editing without performing or being filmed. A dance-trained instructor guides students who choose choreography. Students listen to different views, ask why, explain their reasoning, and compare and revise ideas and wording suggested by AI. By explaining what they made together, they practise critical thinking, discussion, collaboration, and communication in Korean.

Movement before learning, gestures that express word meanings, and activities that involve everyone. Explore the sources behind each idea and how LAB plans to use them.

Harvard Medical School · Naperville · Expert commentary · School practice
Harvard Medical School’s John Ratey explains the relationship between exercise, memory, and concentration. Naperville Central High School ran LRPE, placing physical activity before reading and mathematics classes.
In a Harvard Health interview, John Ratey explains that regular exercise may affect brain regions involved in memory and the neurotrophic factor BDNF. Naperville’s LRPE is a school example focused on this connection between physical activity and learning. A 2013 Illinois Public Health Institute case report describes physical education scheduled before reading and mathematics classes for students who needed learning support.
How LAB designs its classes: This informs our plans for K-POP rhythm and movement before class. We choose activities students can enjoy, then adjust duration and intensity by observing fatigue and participation in the lesson afterward.

Schools on the Move · Finland’s national program
Finland promoted Schools on the Move nationally to add movement during lessons and breaks. School staff reported benefits for learning and the school atmosphere.
Schools on the Move is a program with strategic leadership from Finland’s Ministry of Education and Culture and National Agency for Education, and coordination by JAMK University of Applied Sciences. Rather than a single university experiment, it lets schools increase movement and student participation in ways suited to their circumstances. Official program information and its interim report describe reducing prolonged sitting and involving students in planning activities.
How LAB designs its classes: We connect movement before class with Korean lessons, while preparing after-class co-creation as an optional activity. Roles beyond dance include planning, scripting, and editing, so students can practise listening to and resolving different views.

Max Planck Institute · Vocabulary research in cognitive and brain science
In a 2015 study, participants who performed gestures matching the meanings of unfamiliar words they heard remembered the words better. Meaningful pictures also helped memory.
Researchers at the Max Planck Institute for Human Cognitive and Brain Sciences had participants learn unfamiliar words from an artificial language in several ways. Performing gestures or viewing pictures that matched the meanings helped vocabulary memory compared with listening alone. Watching a movement and performing it produced different results; the connection between the word’s meaning and the movement matters.
How LAB designs its classes: We choose gestures and images that fit the meanings of the Korean being learned. Students use the expressions to describe the order of movements or explain them to classmates, then use them again in cultural projects after class.

These sources inform LAB’s class design. They do not indicate partnerships or accreditation from these institutions, or verified results for LAB’s K-POP classes. LAB’s program is in preparation, and learning outcomes will be assessed during actual operation.

Is after-class co-creation required? — No. Only students who want to join take part in the after-class co-creation program. They can choose planning, scripting, comparing meanings, or editing without dancing, performing, or being filmed. Students decide whether to participate and which role they want.

Has research directly compared exercise and language learning? — A 2007 study by Winter and colleagues compared new vocabulary learning among 27 healthy participants after intense running, low-intensity running, and rest. We refer to it as experimental evidence that exercise conditions can affect vocabulary learning. LAB does not use it as proof of K-POP class outcomes or to claim the same improvement rate for every learner.
